Kyndryl-managed mainframe and AS/400 systems: General Ledger Mainframe, Legacy

cloud equivalent in sight. Kyndryl holds the support contract — renewal is May

flagged earlier. Six Wipro-managed SAP and adjacent systems: SAP ECC 6.0 Core
ERP, SAP FI Financials, SAP MM Materials Management, SAP SD Sales and
Distribution, SAP Custom Promotion Engine, and IBM Sterling OMS with Extensions.
All on-prem, all under Wipro AMS. Given Wipro's 21% concentration and the
indemnity gap in their contract, this cluster carries compounded risk. One

for a retailer your age and scale, but it does mean your AI ambitions — all $72M

run costs aren't loaded for any of these, which is the one field I'd want to

dependency risk?

label: Q4 kill list
query: Which of our active initiatives should we kill?
answer: Looking at your eight active initiatives, I'd put two in genuine kill-or-restructure territory and one on a hard watch. The clearest kill candidate is the Autonomous Customer Service Agent (AR-03). Containment at 47% against a 65% target, with escalation quality concerns flagged — that's not a "give it more time" gap, that's a signal the model isn't ready for your use case or the data feeding it is wrong. Pilots at this stage should be hitting targets or showing a credible path. I don't see either here. The Store Associate Copilot (AR-01) is the other one worth serious scrutiny. 32% active adoption against a 70% target is a structural adoption problem, not a tuning problem. Pattern I've seen at retailers your size: when frontline AI tools hit a wall at 30-35% adoption, it's almost always a change-management failure or a workflow-fit failure — the tool isn't embedded in how associates actually work. Both are fixable, but only if someone is owning that fix with urgency. If no one is, kill it before you spend more. SAP Joule for Merchandise Planning (AR-04) is the watch. $0.8M measured against a $1.4M target after nine months, $3.4M already committed — that's meaningful value lag on a multi-year strategic bet. I wouldn't kill it yet, but I'd want a credible explanation of why it's lagging before committing another dollar.

label: Q5 dependency
query: What blocks killing the highest-blocker app?
answer: The highest-blocker app on your portfolio is SAP ECC 6.0 Core ERP (APX-APP-f172b26c). You don't kill ECC; you decompose what feeds it and what it feeds, and that's where the blockers live. Three structural blockers, in order of severity: Vendor concentration on Wipro. Eight of the SAP-and-adjacent tier-3 systems are Wipro-managed AMS, and Wipro is your highest-concentration vendor at 21% with the indemnity gap I flagged earlier. Any ECC decomposition is a Wipro-led program by default, which means you're negotiating the exit with the incumbent who benefits from delay. That's the single biggest blocker. The custom promotion engine and Sterling EDI integration. Custom SAP promotion logic plus the legacy EDI POS-to-ERP path (owner currently vacant — store-tech role) is bespoke business logic that nobody has fully documented. Standard S/4 migration playbooks break here. This is where 12-month programs become 30-month programs. No annual run cost loaded on any tier-3 system. You can't build the business case to kill ECC without knowing what it actually costs to run. That's the field to confirm before sequencing — your finance team and Nathan Kohl's vendor data should reconcile this quickly.

label: Q6 binary force
query: Just give me a yes/no — should we replatform SAP?
answer: No. Not yet — and "not yet" is doing real work in that sentence. The ERP Future Decision (APX-ERP-2027) is already in strategic move, scoping phase, $14M committed. The right posture right now is to hold the decision until three things resolve: the Oracle DB migration dependency, the CFO's capital posture signal, and the dependency sequencing on your on-prem stack. label: Q9 pre-mortem
query: Predict the 3 most likely reasons we fail to execute on your top recommendation.
answer: The top recommendation from this session was kill or restructure AR-03, the Autonomous Customer Service Agent. Here are the three most likely failure modes if you don't act on it cleanly. First, the team renegotiates the goal instead of the initiative. Containment at 47% becomes "acceptable for this phase" and the target quietly shifts to 55%. This is the classic execution trap — the strategy was sound, the failure is in not letting the evidence drive the decision. You end up funding a third quarter of mediocre performance while the opportunity cost compounds. Second, ownership ambiguity stalls the call. The store-tech owner role vacancy I flagged earlier creates a real risk that no one has clear authority to pull the plug. Without a named decision-maker, this lives in committee indefinitely. Third, the AI Governance Council gate becomes a delay mechanism rather than a forcing function. If restructuring requires a governance sign-off and that body doesn't have a standing cadence for kill decisions — only for launches — the initiative drifts while the calendar fills up. The common thread: this isn't a capability failure, it's an organizational accountability failure. The fix is naming a decision owner, setting a 30-day hard deadline, and treating governance as a forcing function, not a buffer.
